content: 1. Minocycline can reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives, such as conjugated estrogens, by altering intestinal flora. This interaction is specific to oral forms of the hormone. While the risk of contraceptive failure is low, caution and monitoring are advised. 2. Minocycline may decrease the levels or effects of estropipate by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are recommended. 3. Minocycline can reduce the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by altering intestinal flora. This interaction is specific to oral forms of the hormone. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are advised. 4. Lanthanum carbonate can decrease minocycline levels by binding to it in the gastrointestinal tract. To minimize this interaction, oral tetracycline antibiotics should be administered at least 2 hours before or after lanthanum. This interaction applies only to oral tetracyclines. 5. Minocycline may reduce the levels or effects of oral contraceptives containing levonorgestrel, ethinyl estradiol, and ferrous bisglycinate by altering intestinal flora. This interaction is specific to oral forms of the hormone. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are recommended. 6. Magnesium supplements can decrease the absorption of minocycline by forming an insoluble complex in the gastrointestinal tract. To avoid this interaction, magnesium should be taken 2 hours before or 4 hours after minocycline administration. Close monitoring or therapy modification is advised. 7. Minocycline can reduce the levels or effects of mestranol by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are recommended. 8. Minocycline may increase methotrexate levels by reducing its elimination. If tetracyclines cannot be avoided in patients receiving high-dose methotrexate, plasma methotrexate concentrations and signs of toxicity should be closely monitored. 9. Minocycline and methoxsalen may increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, leading to additive photosensitizing effects. Caution and monitoring are advised. 10. Co-administration of minocycline and methylergonovine may increase the toxicity of either drug through an unknown mechanism. Ergot alkaloids and tetracyclines together increase the risk of ergotism. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 11. Minocycline and mipomersen may increase each other's toxicity by potentially elevating hepatic enzymes. Liver function tests (LFTs) should be monitored closely. 12. Minocycline may reduce the effects of piperacillin due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Bacteriostatic agents like minocycline can inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents. Caution and monitoring are advised. 13. Polycarbophil can decrease minocycline levels by inhibiting its gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 14. Minocycline and porfimer may enhance each other's photosensitivity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 15. Minocycline may reduce the effects of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering metabolism. Conversely, these agents can decrease minocycline levels by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. To avoid magnesium chelation, minocycline should be taken at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after these agents. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 16. Concurrent or sequential use of inhaled tobramycin and minocycline may increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Therapy modification or close monitoring is advised to reduce the risk of ototoxicity. 17. Trimagnesium citrate anhydrous can decrease minocycline levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Multivalent cation-containing products may reduce tetracycline bioavailability. Minocycline should be taken at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after magnesium administration. Alternatives should be considered if available. 18. Minocycline and valoctocogene roxaparvovec may increase the risk of hepatotoxicity when combined. Liver enzyme levels should be closely monitored, and alternative medications should be considered in cases of potential drug interactions. 19. Minocycline may increase the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 20. Zinc can decrease minocycline levels by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Oral tetracycline derivatives and oral zinc salts should be administered at least 2 hours apart. Therapy modification or close monitoring is recommended. 21. Minocycline may increase the effects of antithrombin alfa, antithrombin III, and argatroban through pharmacodynamic synergism. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. 22. Minocycline may reduce the levels or effects of balsalazide by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 23. Minocycline may increase the effects of bemiparin, bivalirudin, dalteparin, enoxaparin, fondaparinux, and heparin through pharmacodynamic synergism. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. 24. Minocycline may reduce the levels or effects of biotin, niacin, pantothenic acid, pyridoxine, and thiamine by altering intestinal flora. These interactions apply only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 25. Minocycline may increase the effects of phenindione and protamine through pharmacodynamic synergism. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. 26. Minocycline may reduce the levels of rose hips by increasing elimination. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 27. Sucralfate can decrease minocycline levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 28. Minocycline and verteporfin may increase photosensitivity through pharmacodynamic synergism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 29. Minocycline and vitamin A may increase the risk of benign intracranial hypertension through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution is advised. 30. Minocycline and acitretin are contraindicated due to the risk of increased intracranial pressure. Alternative therapies should be used. 31. Aluminum hydroxide can decrease minocycline levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. These drugs should be separated by 2 hours, or alternative therapies should be used. 32. Minocycline and aminolevulinic acid (oral or topical) may increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, enhancing photosensitivity. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies should be used. 33. Minocycline may reduce the effects of amoxicillin and ampicillin due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Tetracyclines may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins. Alternative therapies should be used, and therapeutic effects should be monitored if co-administered. 34. Minocycline may decrease the effects of cephalosporins (e.g., cefdinir, cefditoren, cefpodoxime, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime) due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Bacteriostatic agents like minocycline can inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents. Close monitoring is recommended. 35. Minocycline and cholera vaccine should not be co-administered due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Systemic antibiotics may inactivate the vaccine strain. Cholera vaccine should not be given to patients who have received antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 36. Cholestyramine can decrease minocycline levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 37. Minocycline and cisatracurium may increase the risk of respiratory depression through pharmacodynamic synergism. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies should be used. 38. Minocycline and dichlorphenamide may increase the risk of metabolic acidosis through pharmacodynamic synergism. Therapy modification or close monitoring is advised. 39. Didanosine can decrease minocycline levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification or close monitoring is recommended.
